seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: My dear Pound: Thanks for your letter and card. I am very sorry to hear that you have been ill. I hope you are now better. I too had an attack of rheumatism which however seems now to have passed.

I wrote at once to Mr Pinker and told him about Drama
.

As regards my novel I agree to your proposal that the passages which the printer will not set up are to be pasted in. You are very kind indeed to undertake such a tiresome work. Miss Weaver says that she will read the proofs. I hope the book will be published and care very little whether it is printed or typewritten so long as it appears.

I have explained my position here to my agent and urged him to try to obtain some advance on my goods – I mean by disposing of the verses (which he has sent to the “English Review”) or the play or the American rights of Dubliners or of the novel. There is no prospect of making any money here except by picking the pockets of the inhabitants so that I hope the grant which was made to me will be renewed. If the intention was to aid me I presume that a renewal will be made but I do not know whether I can take the first step in the matter. I imagine that Yeats and Mr Gosse should do it. It would perhaps be advisable to show to Mr Gosse the novel which is causing everybody (myself included) so much trouble.
I have been obliged to move into new rooms as my landlady let the whole flat of which I had part. Will you please note my new address?

div.note: JJ and family moved from 19 Kreuzstrasse to 54 Seefeldstrasse in Zurich circa 31 March 1916 and remained there until 30 January 1917. Accommodations at this new address were roomier than the previous flat, but still not big enough (LII 376 n.1).
Pound wrote JJ a letter on 16 March 1916 (Pound/Joyce 74-75).

Pound was suffering from sciatica at this time, as he complained to Wyndham Lewis circa March 1916 (Pound/Lewis: The Letters of Ezra Pound and Wyndham Lewis, ed. Timothy Materer [New York: New Directions, 1985], 25).
For JJ’s eye problems and their possible connection with an earlier attack of rheumatic fever, see JJ to Pound, 19 July 1915, notes.

JJ wrote his London literary agent J.B. Pinker on 2 April 1916 that the Chicago review Drama had accepted an article by Pound on JJ’s play, Exiles. The article was published as “Mr. James Joyce and the Modern Stage,” Drama, vol. 6, no. 2 (February 1916): 122-32. (See JJ to Pound, 19 July 1915, notes.) The review declined, however, to publish the play itself, which was eventually published in May 1918 by Grant Richards in London and by B.W. Huebsch in New York.

Pound contrived a scheme, never realized, to have JJ’s A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man printed with blank spaces for controversial passages, which Pound would then supply by personally pasting hand-typed restorations into copies (LII 375-76).

For Pinker’s and Pound’s efforts to place some of JJ’s poems in magazines and to get Exiles produced on the stage and published in print, as well as efforts to find a publisher for A Portrait, see JJ to Pound, 10 March 1916, notes. Dubliners, published by Grant Richards in England in 1914, was first published in the United States by B.W. Huebsch in late 1916.

Authors W.B. Yeats and Edmund Gosse had been instrumental in obtaining for JJ a subsistence grant of £75 from the Royal Literary Fund (see JJ to Pound, 14 July 1915, notes). The grant was not renewed, but in August 1916, with help from Pound, Yeats, and others, JJ obtained a grant of £100 from the British Civil List. JJ also received smaller sums through Pound and the British Society of Authors (Ellmann, JJ 405-06).
